# Debrief guide

<!-- Generated by `npm run benchmarks` from src/shared/materials. Do not edit by hand. -->

What to ask after the last year, what classes usually do, and the numbers behind it.

## What the lesson is for

**Learning goals**

| Goal | What students should come away with |
| --- | --- |
| LG1 | Feel the pull between what is best for you and what is best for the three of you. |
| LG2 | Practise making, keeping and breaking promises, and see what credibility costs. |
| LG3 | Watch trust get built, broken and sometimes repaired, and notice how early moves set the tone. |
| LG4 | Meet best response, the competitive outcome and the cooperative outcome. |
| LG5 | See the price and the profit move with total supply. |
| LG6 | Notice how openness, a surprise new producer and a known final year change behaviour. |

## How to run the debrief

1. End the game, then press **Reveal results to teams** so groups can see the other worlds.
2. Start with **World Comparison** on the projector. Ask the room what they notice before you say anything.
3. Open **World Detail** for the world that held together longest, then for one that did not. Point at the year cooperation broke and ask what happened just before it.
4. Show the **Leaderboard** only after that conversation. Otherwise the room talks about winning rather than about why the money went to buyers.
5. Finish with **Game theory**, using the class’s own numbers, and then the ten questions.

> Use neutral words. No world lost. A world that competed hard made less money and learned the lesson the hard way, which is worth saying out loud.

## The ten questions

**Questions, and where the evidence is**

| # | Question | Goal | Where to look |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Which world came closest to the cooperative maximum, and what did it do differently in Years 1 to 3? | LG1 | the world comparison |
| 2 | In which year did your world's cooperation break, and what happened just before? | LG3 | this world year by year |
| 3 | How did your first decision set the tone for the years that followed? | LG3 | Year 1 in this world |
| 4 | What did your Envoy promise in the messages, and did your group keep it? | LG2 | the messages and what each country did |
| 5 | A new producer arrived in Year 9 with 15.0 million barrels and the price fell. Did that change how much you trusted the others? Did anyone use it as cover for producing more? | LG6 | the price and the new producer |
| 6 | What happened after you were told Year 12 was the final year, and why? | LG6 | the final year |
| 7 | If the other two countries each produce 38.3 million barrels, what is your best output? Why is everyone producing 38.3 not stable? | LG4 | the best response |
| 8 | In which year did the price move most, and why did it move then? | LG5 | the price line |
| 9 | How did your group agree on its number each year? Did whoever was at the keyboard have extra influence? | LG2 | this world year by year |
| 10 | Where outside this classroom do people face this same dilemma? | Transfer | the dilemma in numbers |

## Patterns you will probably see

- Year 1 is usually near the starting number, because nobody has a reason to move yet. Whatever happens in Years 2 and 3 tends to set the tone for the rest.
- A world that talks in numbers in its first chat window usually keeps more of the cooperative maximum than a world that talks in promises without numbers.
- One country going to capacity once is often enough to end an agreement for good, even if it goes back down afterwards.
- The new producer's barrels look exactly like cheating from inside a world. Expect at least one group to accuse another of something nobody did, and ask them how they would have told the difference.
- After the final-year warning most worlds produce more. Ask why a promise is worth less when there is no next year.
- Groups almost always expect the others to produce less than they really do. Ask each world what it assumed, then show the table.

## Answer key

For the standard settings, in Year 1, before any new producer arrives. These are for you, not for the room, until the debrief.

**The two benchmarks**

| Outcome | Each country | Total supply | Price | Each country earns | All three earn |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Everyone cooperates | 38.3 | 114.9 | $35.53 | $1,322.50M | $3,967.50M |
| Everyone competes | 57.5 | 172.5 | $18.25 | $991.88M | $2,975.63M |

The best the three can do together is $3,967.50M a year, at a total of 115.0 million barrels. The debrief scores every world against that number.

### Why the agreement is unstable

If the other two each produce 38.3, your best answer is 75.0 (the formula asks for 76.7, but capacity is 75.0).

    your best output = (a - cost - b x everyone else) / (2 x b)

Doing it earns you $441.50M more than cooperating, and costs each of the other two $421.68M. All three countries can see that same arithmetic, so all three are tempted at once. That is the whole dilemma.

## If you have five minutes left

- Ask where else people face this: queueing, group projects, fishing quotas, revising together, keeping a shared kitchen clean.
- Ask what rule they would add to make cooperation hold, and what it would cost.
- Ask whether they would have behaved differently if the game had run for forty years instead of 12.
